questions.question: The Lighthouse of Alexandria stood on Pharos island for over 1,500 years. What ended it?
options: Rising sea levels that undermined the foundation stones
Deliberate demolition by an incoming Ottoman governor
A series of earthquakes that toppled it over centuries
A fire that consumed the wooden upper structure entirely
questions.answer: A series of earthquakes that toppled it over centuries
questions.explanation: Earthquakes between the 10th and 14th centuries brought it down in stages, and the stone was used to build a fort on the same site. It stood roughly 100 metres and was among the tallest structures on Earth for centuries. Divers found large blocks in Alexandria's harbour in 1994, likely from the lighthouse. The word for lighthouse in French, Spanish and Italian still derives from Pharos.
questions.memory_hook: Earthquakes brought it down in stages between the 10th and 14th centuries, and the stone went into a fort on the same spot. About 100 metres tall, among the tallest things on Earth for centuries. Divers found blocks in the harbour in 1994. French and Spanish still call a lighthouse a phare or faro.

questions.question: The strong nuclear force binds quarks together. What makes it behave unlike gravity?
options: It only operates between particles of identical charge
It weakens to nothing beyond the width of one atom
It gets stronger as quarks are pulled further apart
It acts instantly across any distance in the universe
questions.answer: It gets stronger as quarks are pulled further apart
questions.explanation: Gravity and electromagnetism weaken with distance; the strong force does the opposite between quarks, behaving somewhat like a stretching elastic band. Pull hard enough and the energy invested becomes new quark pairs rather than freeing the original, which is why isolated quarks have never been observed. This is called confinement. The force is roughly 100 times stronger than electromagnetism but acts only across subatomic distances.
questions.memory_hook: Gravity fades with distance; the strong force between quarks does the reverse, like an elastic band. Pull hard enough and the energy just makes new quarks instead of freeing the one you wanted, which is why nobody has ever seen a lone quark. That is confinement.

questions.question: Michael Phelps won 28 Olympic medals. How does that compare to entire countries?
options: More golds than 66 nations have won in their entire history
Fewer golds than any nation that has hosted a Summer Games
Exactly matching the combined total of all African nations
Roughly equal to Australia's total across every sport
questions.answer: More golds than 66 nations have won in their entire history
questions.explanation: Phelps has 23 Olympic golds. Sixty-six countries have won fewer than that across their entire Olympic history, and a further group have never won gold at all. Measured against the nations competing at Rio 2016 he would have ranked ahead of all but 32 of them, one behind host Brazil. He was diagnosed with ADHD as a child, and has since spoken openly about depression following the 2012 Games.
questions.memory_hook: Twenty-three golds, more than 66 countries have managed in their entire Olympic history. Ranked as a nation at Rio he would have finished ahead of all but 32 competing countries, one gold behind Brazil. Diagnosed with ADHD as a child; he has since talked openly about depression after London 2012.

sources.claim: 66 countries have won fewer than Phelps's 23 golds all-time

questions.question: Several actors have played James Bond. What makes counting the films complicated?
options: Three actors played the role in the same year once
Two Bond films were made outside the official series
The first Bond film was made for television, not cinema
Two films were released with two different actors in them
questions.answer: Two Bond films were made outside the official series
questions.explanation: Casino Royale in 1967 was a spoof with David Niven, and Never Say Never Again in 1983 brought Sean Connery back outside the EON series after a long rights dispute over Thunderball. Neither is counted in the official run. Roger Moore appeared in seven official films, one more than Connery's six for EON. Bond was also first played on television in 1954, by American actor Barry Nelson, as Jimmy Bond.
questions.memory_hook: Casino Royale in 1967 was a spoof with David Niven, and Never Say Never Again in 1983 got Connery back outside the official series after a rights fight. Neither counts. Moore did seven official films to Connery's six. And an American played him on TV in 1954, as Jimmy Bond.

questions.question: The Mariana Trench reaches nearly 11km down. How many people have been to the bottom?
options: Around fifty, mostly military submarine crews
Fewer than have walked on the surface of the Moon
None; only uncrewed robotic vehicles have reached it
Several hundred, since commercial dives began in 2015
questions.answer: Fewer than have walked on the surface of the Moon
questions.explanation: Twelve people have walked on the Moon; only a handful have reached Challenger Deep. Piccard and Walsh went first in 1960, James Cameron made a solo dive in 2012, and Victor Vescovo has since made repeat descents. Pressure at the bottom is over 1,000 times surface atmospheric, equivalent to several elephants standing on a postage stamp. Plastic bags and amphipods with plastic in their gut have been found there.
questions.memory_hook: Twelve people have walked on the Moon and only a handful have reached Challenger Deep. Piccard and Walsh in 1960, Cameron alone in 2012, Vescovo repeatedly since. Pressure is over 1,000 atmospheres. They have found plastic bags down there.

questions.question: Nehru became India's first prime minister in 1947. What was Partition's human cost?
options: Between 10 and 20 million displaced and up to a million dead
Around two million displaced with almost no loss of life
Roughly 200,000 relocated under an orderly government scheme
Fewer than 50,000 affected, mostly government employees
questions.answer: Between 10 and 20 million displaced and up to a million dead
questions.explanation: It was among the largest forced migrations in human history, with Hindus and Sikhs moving one way and Muslims the other amid mass violence. Estimates of deaths range from several hundred thousand to a million. The border was drawn in five weeks by Cyril Radcliffe, who had never been to India, and was not published until two days after independence. Kashmir was left unresolved and remains disputed.
questions.memory_hook: Ten to twenty million displaced and estimates up to a million dead, one of the largest forced migrations ever. The border was drawn in five weeks by a man who had never visited India, and published two days after independence. Kashmir was left unresolved and still is.

questions.question: YouTube launched in 2005 and Google bought it a year later. What was it originally meant to be?
options: A live streaming service for independent musicians
A private file-sharing tool for university researchers
An archive for uploading old home movie footage
A video dating site where people posted profile clips
questions.answer: A video dating site where people posted profile clips
questions.explanation: The founders built it as Tune In Hook Up and offered women money to upload dating videos, with no takers, so they opened it to any video at all. The first upload was Me at the zoo, nineteen seconds of a founder at San Diego Zoo. Google paid $1.65 billion in 2006, widely called reckless at the time. Over 500 hours of video are now uploaded every minute.
questions.memory_hook: It was a dating site called Tune In Hook Up, and they offered women money to post dating videos and got nobody, so they opened it to anything. The first upload is nineteen seconds of a founder at San Diego Zoo. Google paid $1.65 billion in 2006 and everyone said they had overpaid.

questions.question: The human body is roughly 60% water. Which organ holds the highest proportion?
options: The liver, at close to 90% by total weight
The stomach, given the fluid it constantly holds
The skin, which is the body's largest organ
The brain and heart, at about 73% water each
questions.answer: The brain and heart, at about 73% water each
questions.explanation: The brain and heart are around 73% water, lungs about 83%, and even bones are roughly 31%. Losing as little as 2% of body water measurably degrades concentration and physical performance, which is why mild dehydration feels like tiredness. The often-repeated eight glasses a day figure has no clear scientific origin, and much of a person's intake comes from food rather than drinks.
questions.memory_hook: Brain and heart are about 73%, lungs 83%, and even bone is 31%. Losing 2% measurably hurts concentration, which is why mild dehydration just feels like being tired. The eight-glasses-a-day rule has no identifiable scientific origin, and a lot of your water comes from food.

questions.question: China has the most natural UNESCO World Heritage sites. What does that designation actually do?
options: Transfers legal ownership of the site to the United Nations
Provides direct UNESCO funding for all conservation work
Bans all tourism and commercial activity at the location
Obliges the state to protect it, with removal as the sanction
questions.answer: Obliges the state to protect it, with removal as the sanction
questions.explanation: Listing commits the country to preserve the site, and the main enforcement is embarrassment: UNESCO can place it on a danger list or delist it entirely. Only a few have ever been removed, including Liverpool's waterfront in 2021 over development, and the Dresden Elbe Valley over a bridge. Ownership stays with the country and funding is limited, so listing mostly confers prestige and tourism revenue.
questions.memory_hook: It commits the country to protect it, and the enforcement is basically shame: danger listing, or removal. Only a handful have ever been delisted, including Liverpool's waterfront in 2021 over development and Dresden over a bridge. Ownership and funding stay with the country.

questions.question: Magellan's expedition first circumnavigated the globe. What happened to Magellan?
options: Killed in the Philippines, so he never completed the voyage
He was arrested for mutiny and executed by his own crew
He completed it and died of fever shortly after returning home
He turned back at the Pacific and sent his deputy onward
questions.answer: Killed in the Philippines, so he never completed the voyage
questions.explanation: Magellan died at Mactan in 1521, roughly halfway. Juan Sebastián Elcano brought one ship home in 1522 with 18 survivors out of about 270 who left. Magellan's Malay slave Enrique may technically have been the first person to circle the globe, since he had been taken from that region originally and returned to it. The crew also lost a day and could not work out why, an early practical encounter with time zones.
questions.memory_hook: He was killed at Mactan in 1521, about halfway. Elcano brought one ship home with 18 of the roughly 270 who left. Magellan's Malay slave Enrique may have been the first to actually circle the globe, since he was taken from that region and came back to it.

questions.question: Moonlight won Best Picture in 2017 after La La Land was announced. How was the error caught?
options: Both films were declared joint winners as a compromise
The Academy issued a correction the following morning
The orchestra stopped playing and the host intervened
A producer read the card and stopped his own speech
questions.answer: A producer read the card and stopped his own speech
questions.explanation: La La Land producer Jordan Horowitz was mid-speech when the error surfaced, held up the correct card to the cameras and said Moonlight had won, handing the statuette over. PwC had duplicate envelopes on both sides of the stage and Warren Beatty was given the wrong one. Both accountants were permanently removed from the ceremony and phones were subsequently banned backstage.
questions.memory_hook: La La Land's producer Jordan Horowitz stopped his own acceptance speech, held the correct card up to the cameras and handed the award over. PwC keeps duplicate envelopes on both sides of the stage and Beatty got the spare. Both accountants were banned from the ceremony afterward.

questions.question: Jim Thorpe won pentathlon and decathlon gold at the 1912 Olympics, then lost both medals. Why?
options: He tested positive for cocaine under new IOC rules
He'd earned $2 a game at semi-pro baseball
He returned them voluntarily to a rival's family
He had competed under a false name after a prior ban
questions.answer: He'd earned $2 a game at semi-pro baseball
questions.explanation: Thorpe had played minor-league baseball for $2/game during summers in 1909-1910 to help support himself — common for poor athletes of the era, but technically a violation of Olympic amateurism rules. A newspaper exposed this in 1913; the IOC demanded the medals back. Thorpe complied. He went on to professional football and baseball careers. He died in poverty in 1953. In 1982, the IOC reversed the decision, citing the 1912 protest deadline (which had been missed) and recognizing the injustice. Replica medals were presented to his family in 1983. His original medals had been distributed to the runners-up — the Swedish copies given to his family are replicas.
questions.memory_hook: Thorpe earned $2/game playing semi-pro baseball to survive — and lost his Olympic medals for it. He died in poverty in 1953. The IOC reversed the decision in 1982, 30 years later, partly because the original protest was filed after the deadline. His family received replicas; the originals had already been given to runners-up. King Gustav V had called him 'the greatest athlete in the world.'
